reply.text:
Two things in that snippet, and only one of them is the leak.

**The leak is the key.** `(job_id, attempt, time.time())` makes every `put` a distinct key, so repeated puts for the same `(job_id, attempt)` — retries, replays, the same job re-run — append instead of overwrite. Combined with no eviction, the dict only grows. That matches the 408k new entries at ~31 MiB.

**The retention serves nothing as written.** `get` returns `hits[-1]`, the last-inserted value for a job. It never reads attempt 1 of 3, never reads anything but the newest. So "keep every attempt for debugging" buys a log's worth of data at the cost of unbounded RSS — a log is where that belongs, not a dict with no ceiling. If the why really is debugging, the fix is to log the attempts and keep one result.

Before I write the change, two checks:

TOOL: grep -rn "ResultCache\|\.put(\|cache\.get(" worker/ --include=*.py | head -40

TOOL: grep -rln "lru_cache\|LRU\|cachetools\|OrderedDict\|def put\|class .*Cache" worker/ lib/ --include=*.py

Why both: the first tells me whether `get` is ever called in a way that needs more than the newest result (if some caller wants an older attempt, keying by `job_id` alone would break it — the "small diff that breaks a caller isn't small" case). The second tells me whether a bounded cache already exists in this codebase, since reusing it beats writing a second one.

“The leak is the key” and “log the attempts and keep one result.”
